review_comments.body:
Those are both offenders.  It’s just the order that should remain stable.

Do you think it would work practically to only fix autocorrection?

I believe the real runs are more complicated, as the corrected file is passed through other cops after correction, and this cuases multiple passes.

For the autocorrect: both subjects are still flagged, I only changed *where* a subject gets moved. Now it moves above preceding `let`s/hooks but stops at another subject — so it never moves one subject above another. If a subject is blocking, it's just not moved on that pass; on the next pass the order is already settled, so it moves then and stays stable.

Would it work if this used `find` on preceeding siblings in reverse order, and would break on first occurrence of `subject`.

I imagine this to be simpler, and slightly more straightforward.
Can you please add a test to cover the nil target?

What used to be a good approach doesn’t work with the new one.
Prevoiusly, we scanned all blocks, and if it was a subject definition, we checked its enclosing parent, and checked all subjects that were not at the top of the enclosing block and moved them up.

With finding just the first one, I believe the methods should be at least named accordingly. It is a first offender, but semantically it’s the only one, because we intend to skip on the other ones, and deal with them in another pass.

Frankly, looking at this, I now have doubts that it used to work the way I imagined it.

If it was scanning for all previous subjects only, it means it used to deal with one at once, not many.

Alternatively, we can do this all in one pass, but the problem would be the reversing that happens due to inserting at the top of the previously corrected ones.

My take: change the iteration to autocorrect in reverse order.

Switched to `reverse_each` with a `break` at the first `subject` (`6729f785`). A plain `find` can't quite express it (we need to stop at the boundary *and* keep the topmost offender before it), but the reverse walk reads much cleaner than the reset-to-nil version.

`'Reports but does not move a subject blocked by a preceding subject'`. There `subject(:b)` is reported but `move_target` returns `nil` on the first pass (blocked by `subject(:a)`), so the `if target` guard is covered. Worth noting the `nil` target is transient — it only shows up mid-convergence, since the blocking subject always moves up on an earlier pass.

Right. The old `offending_node` used `find` with a block that `yield`ed on *every* offending sibling (`add_offense` returns falsy, so `find` never short-circuited), so across passes it hoisted the subject above all preceding lets/hooks — ignoring other subjects as boundaries. That's exactly the bug: with two subjects it lifted both above the lets and could flip their order, and `MultipleSubjects` then dropped the one still in use. The boundary rule fixes that.

Renamed to `preceding_offender` with a doc comment (`6729f785`). I kept it separate from `move_target` on purpose: we still need to report a subject even when its `move_target` is `nil` (blocked by a preceding subject).

I stayed with the multi-pass approach — RuboCop already re-runs to convergence, and it keeps the correction free of manual bookkeeping of shifting insertion points as siblings move. The subject-as-boundary rule preserves relative order across passes. Please tell me if you want to switch to single-pass reverse-order version if you'd prefer one pass, just say the word.
specs should explain this in runnable way
The method name preceding_offender says it all
Why don’t subject(:a) move up first? B could move next. I think that’s the reason we’ve changed the order to reverse

Removed the comment. The behaviour is in the specs now: does not move a subject above another subject, moves several subjects above a preceding hook, keeping their order (three subjects, so the order preservation is visible), and keeps the order of subjects separated by a let.

It does — subject(:a) moves on the first pass and subject(:b) on the next; the expect_correction block is the converged result, both above the hook in their original order. The old name described only the first pass, which was the confusing part, so I renamed it.

The reverse walk in move_target is what makes subject(:a) move first: it breaks at the first preceding subject, so subject(:b) is boundaried by subject(:a) and gets nil until subject(:a) has cleared the slot ahead of it. Moving both in one pass runs into the insert-at-top reversal you flagged on Aug 3 — two subjects moving above the same anchor in a single corrector pass clash. The boundary rule plus RuboCop's convergence loop avoids that: one subject clears the anchor per pass, order preserved. Checked with before; subject(:a); subject(:b); subject(:c) → all three settle above the hook in order.

Is there a test that will fail if we remove ‘if target’? Short yes or no.

Is it a dedicated test? Or would other tests fail due to this side effect?

Short yes or no, no explanation. One sentence.

Rebased onto master (past #2227) while addressing the review.

The Mdformat check is red, but it's failing in the action's own Docker build, not on content: ydah/mdformat-action's Dockerfile runs apt-get upgrade -y on python:3.10-bullseye, and that now 404s on a batch of packages (libperl5.32…deb11u5, libc-dev-bin…deb11u14, linux-libc-dev_5.10.262-1, …) after Debian's latest bullseye point release pruned the old versions from the mirror. It dies before inspecting any file. CHANGELOG.md passes mdformat --check locally and the other 33 checks are green. A re-run once the mirror settles should clear it — I've stopped pushing so as not to burn CI on something the PR can't fix.

> The Mdformat check is red, but it's failing in the action's own Docker build

I opened a PR to fix it: https://github.com/ydah/mdformat-action/pull/15 – cc @ydah

@pirj

Yes. Not dedicated — removing `if target` crashes two existing behavior tests (`does not move a subject above another subject`, `moves several subjects above a preceding hook, keeping their order`) with `NoMethodError: undefined method 'loc' for nil`; the nil branch is a side effect of asserting the final subject order, not something tested in isolation. Verified by pulling the guard locally and running the specs.

On the CHANGELOG line: leaving the current wording. It names the actual failure mode — an autocorrect clash with `RSpec/MultipleSubjects` that could silently drop a subject used in tests — which is what matters to someone deciding whether to run `-A` before reading the diff. Can shorten to your version if you'd still rather have it.

On simplifying further: nothing that keeps `move_target`'s single backward pass. The two-phase result (`subject(:b)` landing correctly) comes from RuboCop re-investigating after `subject(:a)`'s correction is applied, not from anything the method itself tracks — encoding that directly would mean duplicating state the framework already gives for free across passes. Leaving it as is unless you see a concrete cut.

Thanks for the review.

@bquorning your ydah/mdformat-action#15 was merged (2026-09-08), so a re-run of the Mdformat job here should now pass — it was failing in the action's Docker build, not on `CHANGELOG.md`. The other 33 checks are green and the branch is up to date with master.
